# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	// Agent invocation (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §12, §14.6). The executor starts the
2	// agent session with an API CALL rather than by arming a label event, which is
3	// what retires the re-arm, the grace window and the transport dance — and what
4	// makes a lost hand-off a synchronous, visible failure at the executor instead of
5	// a label event fired into the void.
6	//
7	// A TASK NAMES AN ENDPOINT, NEVER A URL. The declaration is vendored verbatim
8	// into every consuming repo, so it must never carry deployment detail or anything
9	// adjacent to a credential: `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` names a key, and the
10	// repo's own config maps that key to a URL and to the NAME of the repo Actions
11	// secret holding its token. That indirection is also what replaces the whole
12	// self/fleet apparatus — reach is a property of which endpoint you call, so a
13	// task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in the
14	// system needs a concept of scope.
15	//
16	// THE PROMPT NAMES ONE ITEM AND CARRIES NO INSTRUCTIONS. Everything
17	// behavior-defining is read by the session from the tracked task files at HEAD;
18	// the prompt says which issue and which nonce, and the session validates both in
19	// code before acting (DESIGN §7).
20	
21	export const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = 'default';
22	
23	// The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/
24	// <trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code
25	// on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller. Three consequences the design's
26	// "a CCR API call" did not spell out, each verified against the routines docs
27	// rather than assumed:
28	//
29	//  - THE BEHAVIOR IS THE ROUTINE'S STORED PROMPT, not ours. `text` reaches the
30	//    session wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block explicitly labelled
31	//    untrusted, and a routine acts on it only because its own saved prompt says
32	//    to. That is the issue-is-data posture arriving for free at one more hop: our
33	//    payload names an item, and every instruction comes from a stored artifact.
34	//    The routine's stored prompt is one line pointing at `instructions.md` beside
35	//    this file, so the whole of what a session does is tracked and reviewed.
36	//  - THE BODY CARRIES ONE FIELD. `text` is freeform and unparsed — structured
37	//    JSON would arrive as a literal string — so the item number and nonce go in
38	//    as prose, and nothing else goes in at all.
39	//  - THERE IS NO IDEMPOTENCY KEY (standing entry 11, answered: the endpoint
40	//    offers none), which is exactly why THIS MODULE CALLS ONCE PER ITEM AND NEVER
41	//    RETRIES. A retry is only safe when you know the first call did nothing, and
42	//    a client-side timeout is the one case where you cannot know — the session
43	//    may well have started. Retrying there is what would make invocation
44	//    at-least-once and put two sessions on one item; declining to retry is what
45	//    keeps it at-most-once and lets the whole agent-side claim protocol delete.
46	//    An outcome we did not learn is reported as UNKNOWN and resolved by the agent
47	//    leash, which is a rule that already exists, rather than by a guess here.
48	//
49	// The beta header is dated and the endpoint is a research preview whose two most
50	// recent header versions keep working, so it lives in config with a default here
51	// — a rotation is then a config edit on one repo, never an engine release the
52	// whole fleet waits for.
53	export const DEFAULT_HEADERS = Object.freeze({
54	  'anthropic-beta': 'experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01',
55	  'anthropic-version': '2023-06-01',
56	});
57	
58	// The endpoint a task's hand-off calls, resolved against the repo's config.
59	// Returns `{ name, url, tokenEnv, headers }` or `{ name, error }` — a task naming
60	// an endpoint the repo has not configured is a repo-configuration fact, reported
61	// where the operator reads it, never a crash.
62	export function resolveEndpoint(config, task) {
63	  const name = task?.decl?.invocation_endpoint ?? DEFAULT_ENDPOINT;
64	  const endpoints = config?.taskScheduler?.endpoints ?? {};
65	  const entry = endpoints[name];
66	  if (!entry) {
67	    return { name, error: `this repo's config declares no invocation endpoint "${name}" (taskScheduler.endpoints)` };
68	  }
69	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
70	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
71	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
72	}
73	
74	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
75	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
76	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
77	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
78	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
79	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
80	// more than a label event was.
81	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
82	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
83	
84	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
85	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
86	//
87	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
88	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
89	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
90	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
91	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
92	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
93	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
94	//                                         guess which.
95	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
96	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
97	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
98	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
99	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
100	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
101	    if (!token) {
102	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
103	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
104	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
105	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
106	    }
107	
108	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
109	
110	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
111	    try {
112	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
113	        method: 'POST',
114	        headers: {
115	          ...endpoint.headers,
116	          'content-type': 'application/json',
117	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
118	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
119	        },
120	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
121	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
122	      });
123	      let json = null;
124	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
125	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
126	        return {
127	          ok: true,
128	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
129	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
130	        };
131	      }
132	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
133	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
134	      return {
135	        ok: false, answered: true,
136	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
137	      };
138	    } catch (e) {
139	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
140	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
141	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
142	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
143	    }
144	  };
145	}

# Dedup local packs against the canon

The **method** of the growth lifecycle's pruning stage: reconcile a repo's own **local packs**
(`.claudinite/local/packs/`; legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename
window) against the shared canon it consumes, pruning local items the canon now covers. Two
callers share it: the unattended [growth-dedup task](../../tasks/growth-dedup/task.md) (which
frames the run — dispatch, the human-gated PR, tracking issue), and an owner asking in-session
to reconcile local packs against the canon. Often there's nothing to prune, and that's fine.

**The yardstick is the mounted canon** — the exact revision the repo currently consumes, what
`.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp — never a live fetch (a promotion is visible
here only once baselining has converged the mount to include it). The mount is never a prune
*target*, only what you prune *against*.

## The three actions — every one removes portable text

- **Remove** a now-duplicated local item, since the canon is the single source of truth for
  portable rules.
- **Strip** a *partially* covered item down to its residue — when an item's general half is now
  canon-owned but it still carries a stronger point about a narrower case, **delete the portable
  half in place and keep only the residue**. A strip is a **deletion that shrinks the entry**:
  lead with the residual point (using the file's own `(canon)` tag convention if it has one),
  never with a meta-line like "this rule is portable (canon)", and **never re-state the
  now-canon rule, its fix, or which pack owns it** — carrying it is exactly what you are
  removing. If your "strip" adds words or restates the canon, you have *un*-deduped the item:
  keep the pre-edit text instead.
- **Rephrase** a local procedure *only* when the canon's wording of the same idea has changed,
  so the local packs stay consistent with the canon they point at — a rephrase tracks a wording
  drift; it never grows the entry and never re-imports canon prose.

An edit that leaves an entry the same size or larger, re-quotes the now-canon rule, or names the
owning pack's fix is a **corruption, not a dedup**. When in doubt about a kept item, leave it
byte-for-byte unchanged rather than "reconcile" its wording. The `dedup-prune-integrity` check
([dedup-integrity.mjs](../../dedup-integrity.mjs)) is the machine backstop: it reds the session
when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file, or when any change adds a line that
restates a canon rule.

## The keep-test: says *more*, not merely says it more specifically

Every local item is more specific than the canon, so specificity alone is never the test.
Distinguish two cases:

- **The general rule in local dress** — it makes the canon's point but leans on this repo's
  classes, files, or names to make it. Once the canon covers the point, those names were only
  illustration: prune it.
- **A stronger point about a narrower case** — it asserts something the canon's general rule
  leaves out: a tighter constraint, a sharper claim that holds for this repo's narrower
  situation. Keep it.

So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the
general point, or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.

## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose

The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when
a canon check *enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every
session and CI pass. Consult the machine-readable rule catalog
(`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`: id, severity, description,
doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose corpus, and
when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line.
This cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the
same rule — prune the local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd
prune a duplicated prose line. The keep-test above is unchanged.

## Discipline

- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon
  line (or the covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a
  real local lesson.
- **Write only inside the local packs.** A dedup run's whole surface is
  `.claudinite/local/packs/` — never the canon it prunes against, never the project's own code. The
  `growth-write-scope` check ([growth-write-scope.mjs](../../growth-write-scope.mjs)) keys on the
  run's pinned `Claudinite growth: dedup local packs` title and reds any path outside that surface.
- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green
  before delivering.

# vascular-coloring — this repo's own pack

The **vessel-image quantification** domain this project works in: gP-CD31 (red) confocal panels
measured for categorize / count / measure. A local pack — declared by hand as
`local/vascular-coloring` in `.claudinite-checks.json`, never fingerprinted.

It carries only what the canon doesn't: `research-project` already owns the class (run an algorithm
over similarly-formatted inputs, score against ground truth, iterate visibly), so the loop, the
ground-truth discipline and the anti-overfitting stance are **not** repeated here. What is here is
imaging-specific and concrete — the palette the red signal forces, the render-vs-data commit line,
the calibration without which a micrometre is not a micrometre, and the locked metric fields that
keep every recorded number meaning the same thing.

## Checks (`rules`)

| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `overlay-color-contrast` | no red marks on red signal | blocking |
| `rendered-overlays-untracked` | rendered overlays stay uncommitted | blocking |
| `panel-scale-calibration` | every working figure stays calibrated | blocking |
| `scale-numbers-match-calibration` | quoted µm/px matches its source | blocking |
| `locked-metric-fields` | locked metrics stay reported | blocking |
| `calibration-single-source` | one calibration table, imported | blocking |
| `render-outputs-gitignored` | render directories stay ignored | blocking |

Fixtures: [`pack.test.mjs`](pack.test.mjs) — each check shown firing on a violating input and quiet
on a clean one (`node .claudinite/local/packs/vascular-coloring/pack.test.mjs`).

## Prose (`RULES.md`)

| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
|---|---|
| Never validate pipeline against itself | prose |
| Progress is a visual assertion | prose (+ the `vessel-overlay-review` skill) |
| Metric definitions are locked | prose (+ `locked-metric-fields`) |
| Raw length not cross-comparable | prose (+ `panel-scale-calibration`, `scale-numbers-match-calibration`, `calibration-single-source`) |
| A paper is read once, written down | prose (+ the `paper-intake` skill) |
| Say which numbers are trustworthy | prose |

## Skills

| Skill | Trigger |
|---|---|
| [vessel-overlay-review](skills/vessel-overlay-review/SKILL.md) | proposing, revising or reporting on the extraction pipeline |
| [paper-intake](skills/paper-intake/SKILL.md) | a research paper is added to `references/`, or one needs re-processing |

Distilled from this repo's real usage: [`analysis/WORKING-GUIDE.md`](../../../../analysis/WORKING-GUIDE.md),
[`analysis/annotate_overlays.py`](../../../../analysis/annotate_overlays.py),
[`analysis/measure_vessels.py`](../../../../analysis/measure_vessels.py), the `.gitignore` render
exclusions, and the 16 `VESSEL_*` panels under
[`references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels`](../../../../references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels).

4	---
5	
6	# Paper intake
7	
8	The owner adds articles so the project can keep working **without reopening them**. An intake is
9	finished when someone could delete the PDF and lose nothing they need: the biology, the method,
10	the parameters, the numbers, and every figure are all in the repo, described.
11	
12	Layout, slug format and the working-dataset contract: [`references/README.md`](../../../../../../references/README.md).
13	Cross-paper decisions: [`references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md`](../../../../../../references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md).
14	
15	## The steps
16	
17	### 1. Place the paper
18	
19	Slug is `<first-author>-<year>-<short-topic>`. Create `references/<slug>/` and `git mv` the PDF in
20	as `<slug>.pdf` — the original file keeps its content but not its unwieldy download name.
21	
22	### 2. Extract text and images
23	
24	```
25	python3 references/_tools/extract_pdf_assets.py references/<slug>/<slug>.pdf /tmp/<slug>
26	```
27	
28	Writes `fulltext.txt`, `raw/` and `manifest.tsv`. **Work from the scratchpad**, not the repo —
29	only named, described figures get committed.
30	
31	### 3. Chase the supplementary material — it is often where the method actually lives
32	
33	**Ask for it if it is not to hand.** Rust 2020's main text leaves the binarization method, the
34	filter radius, the particle-size floor and the heatmap grid all unstated; its supplementary Data
35	Sheet supplied every one of them, plus the verbatim macro and a **µm-calibrated native-resolution
36	vessel image** that became the best input in the repo and the basis of the strongest validation
37	the project has. That material was one download away and the digest was materially wrong without it.
38	
39	Commit supplementary code, scripts, LUTs and data images under
40	`references/<slug>/supplementary/`. Transcribe supplementary *tables* into the digest.
41	
42	### 4. Read the whole paper
43	
44	Read `fulltext.txt` end to end. Then **look at every extracted image** — do not skip this. Papers
45	put their method in figures: Rust 2020's entire pipeline specification exists only as pixels in
46	Figure 1C. Anything that is only in an image and matters must be **transcribed into the digest**.
47	
48	### 5. Name and commit the figures
49	
50	`git mv` each real figure to `references/<slug>/figures/figN_<short-name>.png` (convert to PNG).
51	Drop logos, glyphs and icons. Write `figures/README.md`: every figure **shown inline**
52	(`![Figure 1](fig1_….png)`) with a description of each sub-panel, what the scale bars say, and
53	**what you actually see in it** — including anything that will trip the pipeline up (surface
54	vessels, drawn annotation lines, cross-sections rather than networks).
55	
56	### 6. Crop the panels
57	
58	Locate the grid programmatically where possible (photomicrograph panels are dark, the page is
59	white — find the dark bands), then **freeze the coordinates** into
60	`references/<slug>/figures/crop_panels.py` so the crop is reproducible. Prefix the isolated
61	vessel-channel panels `VESSEL_` and nothing else. Tag every panel name with the paper
62	(`rust20fig1_…`) so calibration prefixes stay unique. Write `figures/panels/README.md`: the
63	inventory, the µm/px per row, and the caveats that come with folding these into the dataset.
64	
65	### 7. Calibrate — measure, never assume
66	
67	**Measure the drawn scale bar in pixels off the panel itself** and add the prefix to
68	`SCALEBAR_PX` in `analysis/measure_vessels.py` (plus `SCALEBAR_UM` if the bar is not 50 µm).
69	Never derive µm/px from a stated field-of-view, and never carry a number over from a
70	neighbouring row.
71	
72	If the source image **states its own µm/px** (an ImageJ TIFF carries `unit=` and `XResolution`),
73	use that instead and record it in `UMPP_DIRECT` with its provenance — acquisition metadata is
74	better evidence than a bar measured off a printed page. **Cross-check it against biology** before
75	trusting it: capillaries should come out at roughly 4–8 µm across.
76	
77	If a figure draws **no** bar, put the prefix in `UNCALIBRATED` **with the reason**. That panel
78	then reports area % and pixels only. All three tables are checked by `panel-scale-calibration`.
79	
80	Cross-check when the figure lets you: a close-up's ROI box in its overview gives an independent
81	magnification estimate. **Record the agreement, and record it when it is poor** — that is a real
82	uncertainty in every length the panel produces.
83	
84	### 8. Write the digest
85	
86	`references/<slug>/digest.md`. It must stand alone. Always include:
87	
88	- **Citation block** — title, authors, venue, DOI, licence, link to the PDF, one-line thesis.
89	- **§ Why this matters to *our* task** — first, and concrete. What does this paper change about
90	  what we build? What does it explicitly *not* cover?
91	- **The method, in full.** Every parameter the paper states. Every parameter it *fails* to state,
92	  listed as a gap, so nobody re-hunts.
93	- **The reported numbers**, in tables, with the stats.
94	- **Calibration facts** for the extracted panels, with the caveats from step 7.
95	- **Discussion arguments worth keeping**, and the authors' own stated limitations.
96	- **§ What is not in this PDF** — supplementary material, scripts, anything you tried to fetch and
97	  could not (record the URL and what happened).
98	- **§ Extracted images** — the figure table, linked.
99	
100	### 9. Fold into the synthesis
101	
102	Update [`references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md`](../../../../../../references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md): add
103	the paper to the folded-in list, extend the metric and processing tables, add reference
104	magnitudes, and — most valuable — **compare the published numbers to ours and say what the gap
105	means**. A published branch density 5× below ours is a sharper statement of our fragmentation
106	problem than any overlay.
107	
108	Add the paper's row to [`references/README.md`](../../../../../../references/README.md).
109	
110	### 10. Verify
111	
112	```
113	python3 analysis/measure_vessels.py                                   # new panels appear, µm sane
114	node .claudinite/local/packs/vascular-coloring/pack.test.mjs          # checks still pass
115	```
116	
117	## The rules that bite here
118	
119	- **Never invent a number.** Not a scale bar, not a field size, not a metric. Measure it, cite it,
120	  or declare it unknown. This is the project's first rule and intake is where it is most tempting
121	  to break.
122	- **The pipeline's own output is never ground truth** for a new panel set. A digest may quote what
123	  the *authors* measured; it must not present our run over their images as validation.
124	- **Say what is weak.** A calibration you half-trust, a panel type the metrics do not suit, a
125	  direction-of-change that contradicts another paper — all of it goes in the digest. The digests
126	  are read later by someone deciding what to believe.
127	- **Different papers are never averaged together.** Species, model, marker and magnification all
128	  differ; the rollup is grouped per paper for that reason.
129	- **Prefer a same-image comparison to a table comparison.** If the paper ships code *and* an
130	  image, reimplement the method and run both on that image. Comparing our figure-crop output to a
131	  published summary table produced a confident, wrong conclusion about our branch counts; running
132	  the authors' own macro on their own image corrected it. A number from a summary table may not
133	  be the raw output of the method it describes.

# Paper intake

The owner adds articles so the project can keep working **without reopening them**. An intake is
finished when someone could delete the PDF and lose nothing they need: the biology, the method,
the parameters, the numbers, and every figure are all in the repo, described.

`references/<slug>/supplementary/`. Transcribe supplementary *tables* into the digest.

### 4. Read the whole paper

Read `fulltext.txt` end to end. Then **look at every extracted image** — do not skip this. Papers

### 5. Name and commit the figures

(`rust20fig1_…`) so calibration prefixes stay unique. Write `figures/panels/README.md`: the
inventory, the µm/px per row, and the caveats that come with folding these into the dataset.

### 7. Calibrate — measure, never assume

**Measure the drawn scale bar in pixels off the panel itself** and add the prefix to

neighbouring row.

If the source image **states its own µm/px** (an ImageJ TIFF carries `unit=` and `XResolution`),
use that instead and record it in `UMPP_DIRECT` with its provenance — acquisition metadata is
better evidence than a bar measured off a printed page. **Cross-check it against biology** before
trusting it: capillaries should come out at roughly 4–8 µm across.

If a figure draws **no** bar, put the prefix in `UNCALIBRATED` **with the reason**. That panel
then reports area % and pixels only. All three tables are checked by `panel-scale-calibration`.

Cross-check when the figure lets you: a close-up's ROI box in its overview gives an independent
magnification estimate. **Record the agreement, and record it when it is poor** — that is a real
uncertainty in every length the panel produces.

### 8. Write the digest

`references/<slug>/digest.md`. It must stand alone. Always include:

- **Citation block** — title, authors, venue, DOI, licence, link to the PDF, one-line thesis.
- **§ Why this matters to *our* task** — first, and concrete. What does this paper change about
  what we build? What does it explicitly *not* cover?
- **The method, in full.** Every parameter the paper states. Every parameter it *fails* to state,

- **The reported numbers**, in tables, with the stats.

- **§ What is not in this PDF** — supplementary material, scripts, anything you tried to fetch and

2	name: vessel-overlay-review
3	description: Show a vessel-extraction result as an annotated overlay on the original panel and state explicit visual assertions about it. Use whenever proposing, revising, or reporting on the segmentation/measurement pipeline in this repo — before quoting any new numbers.
4	---
5	
6	# Reviewing a vessel extraction on the overlay
7	
8	The owner reacts to **pictures with claims attached**, not to metric tables. Any change to
9	`analysis/measure_vessels.py` (segmentation, pruning, branch graph, caliber threshold) is presented
10	this way before its numbers are quoted.
11	
12	## 1. Regenerate
13	
14	```
15	python3 analysis/measure_vessels.py                  # per-image + region metrics table
16	python3 analysis/annotate_overlays.py [name-substr]  # presentation overlays -> analysis/annotated/
17	```
18	
19	Both output directories hold renders, not data: regenerate them, never commit their PNGs
20	(`render-outputs-gitignored` keeps every render directory ignored by git,
21	`rendered-overlays-untracked` catches a PNG that got committed anyway). Setup:
22	`pip install -r requirements.txt`.
23	
24	## 2. Keep the agreed overlay style
25	
26	`analysis/annotate_overlays.py` is the source of truth for it, and it is the style the owner
27	iterated to — change it only on request:
28	
29	- overlay on the **original at full brightness**; the debug 3-panel view in `measure_vessels.py`
30	  (`--overlays`) may dim, the presentation overlay may not;
31	- a highlight is a **slim outline that circles the thing — never a colour fill**; contours drawn at
32	  display resolution, 1 px, alpha-blended so the signal reads through;
33	- colours contrast with the red channel — cyan capillary, green artery, magenta junction, yellow
34	  labels. **No red overlay marks** (`overlay-color-contrast` enforces this);
35	- arrows label representative vessels with their length in µm, one artery with its diameter; a drawn
36	  50 µm bar and a totals banner (segments cap/artery, length + density, junctions, area %).
37	
38	## 3. State the assertions
39	
40	Alongside the overlay, write the claims a reader can check against it, in both directions:
41	
42	- **what the method caught** — "each cyan outline is one segment I counted";
43	- **what it missed or broke** — "the red vessel at lower-left carries no outline: under-detection in
44	  this dim field"; "this vessel is split into three segments by a stain dropout, so COUNT is
45	  inflated here".
46	
47	A review that only shows the good fields is not a review. Compare against the visual expectations in
48	`references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels/expected-results.md` — never against the pipeline's own previous output.
49	
50	## 4. Then the numbers
51	
52	Use **length density / area %** for anything cross-figure (the
53	figures are at different zoom). Record the accepted change and its metric delta in
54	`analysis/results-first-pass.md`, and refresh `analysis/STATUS.md`'s "trustworthy vs not" and next
55	step so the next session resumes from it.

70	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
71	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.

74	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by

150

152	|---|---|---|
153	| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
154	| `dedup-prune-integrity` | work-scope ([dedup-integrity.mjs](dedup-integrity.mjs)) | a dedup edit only removes portable text — never grows a local pack or re-imports a canon rule |

157	The capture runs' write surface is the local packs and nothing else — a run improves the repo's
158	**packs**, never the canon it prunes against or the project's own code. `growth-write-scope` is
159	the machine guarantee behind that, keyed on the pinned commit titles of exactly those two runs; the
160	lifecycle's wider-surfaced runs have their own gates (promote writes the canon under `packs/` and

167	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new

170	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
171	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
172	task's job.
173	
174	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
175	
176	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
177	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
178	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
179	project's own content;
180	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
181	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
182	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
183	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
184	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
185	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
186	
187	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
188	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
189	failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
190	what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
191	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
192	
193	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
194	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
195	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
196	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
197	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.

| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
| `dedup-prune-integrity` | work-scope ([dedup-integrity.mjs](dedup-integrity.mjs)) | a dedup edit only removes portable text — never grows a local pack or re-imports a canon rule |
| `growth-write-scope` | work-scope ([growth-write-scope.mjs](growth-write-scope.mjs)) | a capture run (extract, dedup) writes only the repo's own local packs |

The capture runs' write surface is the local packs and nothing else — a run improves the repo's
**packs**, never the canon it prunes against or the project's own code. `growth-write-scope` is
the machine guarantee behind that, keyed on the pinned commit titles of exactly those two runs; the
lifecycle's wider-surfaced runs have their own gates (promote writes the canon under `packs/` and
`skills/`, certified by canon-curation's `promote-scope`; pack discovery also writes the repo-root
declaration that activates the pack it authors).

**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
task's job.

## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)

Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
project's own content;
the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).

Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.

The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.

56	  comments stay free to mention — or quote paths into — the barred folders; the coupling class
57	  this scope polices is the one that crashes at runtime. Default is every resolvable reference;
58	  incompatible with `matchNames` (a text layer an imports-only edge excludes by definition).
59	- **`allow: [...]`** (or a single `"allow": "shared"`) — folders reachable despite the ban (a `shared`/`contracts` folder both sides may use). Always implicitly allowed: references *within* the guarded region itself.
60	- **`matchNames: true`** — opt into the **bare-name layer**: the barred folders' own names are matched as bare words too (see below). `alsoMatchNames: [...]` force-includes non-distinctive names.
61	- **`matchUniqueFilenames: false`** — opt *out* of the unique-basename layer (on by default). 62	- **`except: [...]`** — the rule's own exceptions (see [Exceptions](#exceptions-carve-outs-and-reviewed-crossings)).
63	- **`reason`** — surfaced as the finding's *why*.
64	
65	Paths are repo-relative prefixes; both `/` and `\` separators are accepted. A malformed rule — overlapping `from`/`to`, an empty prefix, an unknown property — is a blocking `config` finding, not a silent no-op.
66	
67	### The whole-repo form
68	
69	`from: "."` guards the entire repo, carved down by `except` carve-out strings. It is the safe-by-default posture (a new top-level file is guarded until excepted), at the cost of listing the content trees to subtract:
70	
71	```json
72	{ "from": ".", "to": "plugins/*", "matchNames": true,
73	  "except": ["plugins/*", "plugins/README.md"],
74	  "reason": "the host must not know the specific plugins it loads" }
75	```
76	
77	The repo root must be spelled `.` explicitly (`""`/`"/"` are rejected as likely typos), and every barred target must lie inside a carve-out — otherwise the self-reference rule would exempt it, so the rule is rejected as a `config` error rather than silently under-enforcing. 80	
81	The unit of detection is *a reference that resolves to a real tracked path inside the barred folder*. That single rule is what makes it language-agnostic and precise:
82	
83	1. **Candidate extraction** — on every line of every guarded file (comments and Markdown included): quoted strings (import specifiers, `require()`, `@import`, config values, JSON) **and** unquoted path-ish tokens. 84	2. **Resolution against the repo tree** — a candidate resolves via, in order: file-relative (`../server/db.js`, `..\server\db.js`), repo-root-relative (`server/db.js`), Python-style *absolute* dotted module (`import server.pkg.mod` → `server/pkg/mod.py`), then the unique-basename layer. 86	
87	**The bare-name layer** (opt-in, `matchNames: true`): a barred folder's own *name* is matched as a bare word — in prose, a backtick cite, a string literal — and resolves to that folder. 88	
89	**In scope for v1:** imports and path strings that resolve into the barred folder, plus unique `filename.ext` mentions — anywhere, comments and docs included — plus opted-in bare names. Vendored/generated files are excluded automatically (the runner drops them from `ctx.files`).
90	
91	### Known limitations
92	
93	The engine is **best-effort for imports and precise (no false positives) by design** — it would rather miss an exotic reference form than block on a guess. It does *not* resolve, and so does not catch, these crossings (a follow-up may add them; each needs real per-language handling):
94	
95	- **Plain-word folder names** in prose (`"see the server module"`). Distinctive names are the `matchNames: true` layer's job; single ordinary words are only matched when force-included via `alsoMatchNames`, because English can't be told apart from an identifier.
96	- **Class/function symbol references** (a `from`-file *using* a symbol *defined* in `to`). Needs per-language symbol extraction and resolution.
97	- **Python *relative* imports** (`from ..server import x`) and **`from x import y`** name imports. Only the absolute dotted form (`import server.x`) resolves today.
98	- **Alias imports** (`@/server/db`, `~/server/db`, tsconfig/webpack `paths`). The engine has no project alias map.
99	- **Rust `::` paths** (`use crate::server::db;`).

103	
104	## Exceptions: carve-outs and reviewed crossings
105	
106	A rule's `except` array holds two kinds of entry, and a rule owns both — there is no separate top-level accept list.
107	
108	**Carve-out strings** subtract files from the guarded region — they are not scanned, *and* references to them stop counting as self-references (the mechanism that makes `from: "."` coherent). Entries are folders/files, `"<folder>/*"` child-directory globs, or `"*.suffix"` name patterns:
109	
110	```json
111	"except": ["plugins/*", "plugins/README.md", "*.generated.js"]
112	```
113	
114	**Reviewed exceptions** `{ path, to?, reason }` excuse a deliberate crossing, reviewed once like any code:
115	
116	```json
117	"except": [
118	  { "path": "engine/registry.js", "to": ["plugins/legacy"],
119	    "reason": "temporary bridge during the plugin split — tracked in #123" },
120	  { "path": "docs/inventory.md",
121	    "reason": "historical ledger — it enumerates the plugins it catalogs by name" }
122	]
123	```
124	
125	- **`path`** — one file, or a subtree with a trailing `/`.
126	- **`to`** — the barred folder(s) this file may reference. **With `to`**, the exception is *pinned*: a crossing from that file to a *different* barred folder still fails, so no new coupling slips into an already-reviewed file. **Without `to`**, it excuses every crossing from that file — a whole-file exemption for a genuinely enumerative file (a ledger), carrying a reason a bare carve-out string can't.
127	- **`reason`** — required. It is what makes the crossing reviewable.
128	
129	On a whole-repo sweep with a clean config, an exception that matched **nothing** is itself a blocking finding: the coupling it excused is gone, so the entry (or the unused `to` item) gets pruned instead of rotting. 130	
131	(The runner's generic top-level `accept` — `{ "rule": "barrier", "path": "...", "reason": "..." }` — still works too, retiring *every* barrier finding in a file. Prefer a rule's own `except`: it is pinned per target and staleness-audited, where the generic accept is a silent whole-file waiver.)
132	
133	## Composing a barrier from another pack
134	
135	A pack ships a *fixed* barrier — no project config needed — by **declaring** this pack and **contributing** the barrier as data on its manifest, never by importing this pack's code (`pack-independence`): name `barriers` in the pack's `requires` and carry the barrier under `contributes`:
136	
137	```js
138	// packs/<somepack>/pack.mjs
139	export default {
140	  id: 'somepack',
141	  requires: ['barriers'],
142	  contributes: {
143	    barriers: [{
144	      id: 'requirements-isolation',
145	      edges: [{ from: 'dev/requirements', to: '*', reason: 'requirements is a pure sink' }],
146	    }],
147	  },
148	};
149	```
150	
151	Each contribution becomes a **first-class rule under its own id** — per-rule overrides (`rules: { "requirements-isolation": "off" }`) and acceptances address it directly, and `description`/`why`/`doc`/`severity`/`crossingRemedy`/`crossingExcuse` ride the contribution. The two `crossing*` fields own the halves of a crossing finding's `fix`: `crossingRemedy` replaces the default "route shared code through …" opener where relocating the dependency isn't the way out (a one-sided isolation edge has no shared folder to route through), and `crossingExcuse` names the excusal lever that actually works for a pack-shipped edge. Write the remedy into one of these, not into `description` — a rendered finding carries `what`/`why`/`fix`/`doc` and never the rule's description. `gateDir` is the one declarative gate: the rule stays inert until that directory exists in the repo under test (how the baseline's consumer-isolation wall stays quiet pre-flip). The runner hands this pack the active-pack list (`contributedRules` on its manifest, the generic core seam), and [contributed.mjs](contributed.mjs) builds the rules — an undeclared pack contributes nothing, exactly as its own rules would not run. A consumer's local pack contributes the same way. A helper a pack needs beside a barrier (path containment, say) lives in the engine lib (`engine/checks/helpers/path-containment.mjs`), never in this pack's modules.

- **Alias imports** (`@/server/db`, `~/server/db`, tsconfig/webpack `paths`). The engine has no project alias map.
- **Rust `::` paths** (`use crate::server::db;`).
- **Case-only differences** on case-insensitive filesystems (`../Server/db.js`). Matching is case-sensitive — the same behavior a Linux CI runtime has.

One precision caveat cuts the other way: the unique-basename layer can resolve a **convention marker name** (a `RULES.md`-like filename every sibling is *meant* to carry) while only one folder happens to carry it yet. Such a hit is a false coupling — set **`matchUniqueFilenames: false`** on the rule to turn the layer off (path references and distinctive names still fire), or, if you want to keep the layer for other files, accept the one crossing with an exception whose reason says so.

## Exceptions: carve-outs and reviewed crossings

A rule's `except` array holds two kinds of entry, and a rule owns both — there is no separate top-level accept list.

**Carve-out strings** subtract files from the guarded region — they are not scanned, *and* references to them stop counting as self-references (the mechanism that makes `from: "."` coherent). Entries are folders/files, `"<folder>/*"` child-directory globs, or `"*.suffix"` name patterns:

```json
"except": ["plugins/*", "plugins/README.md", "*.generated.js"]
```

**Reviewed exceptions** `{ path, to?, reason }` excuse a deliberate crossing, reviewed once like any code:

```json
"except": [
  { "path": "engine/registry.js", "to": ["plugins/legacy"],
    "reason": "temporary bridge during the plugin split — tracked in #123" },
  { "path": "docs/inventory.md",
    "reason": "historical ledger — it enumerates the plugins it catalogs by name" }
]
```

- **`path`** — one file, or a subtree with a trailing `/`.
- **`to`** — the barred folder(s) this file may reference. **With `to`**, the exception is *pinned*: a crossing from that file to a *different* barred folder still fails, so no new coupling slips into an already-reviewed file. **Without `to`**, it excuses every crossing from that file — a whole-file exemption for a genuinely enumerative file (a ledger), carrying a reason a bare carve-out string can't.
- **`reason`** — required. It is what makes the crossing reviewable.

On a whole-repo sweep with a clean config, an exception that matched **nothing** is itself a blocking finding: the coupling it excused is gone, so the entry (or the unused `to` item) gets pruned instead of rotting. Shrinking a rule's reviewed exceptions to none is the definition of "the graph holds."

(The runner's generic top-level `accept` — `{ "rule": "barrier", "path": "...", "reason": "..." }` — still works too, retiring *every* barrier finding in a file. Prefer a rule's own `except`: it is pinned per target and staleness-audited, where the generic accept is a silent whole-file waiver.)

## Composing a barrier from another pack

A pack ships a *fixed* barrier — no project config needed — by **declaring** this pack and **contributing** the barrier as data on its manifest, never by importing this pack's code (`pack-independence`): name `barriers` in the pack's `requires` and carry the barrier under `contributes`:

```js
// packs/<somepack>/pack.mjs
export default {
  id: 'somepack',
  requires: ['barriers'],
  contributes: {
    barriers: [{
      id: 'requirements-isolation',
      edges: [{ from: 'dev/requirements', to: '*', reason: 'requirements is a pure sink' }],
    }],
  },
};
```

Each contribution becomes a **first-class rule under its own id** — per-rule overrides (`rules: { "requirements-isolation": "off" }`) and acceptances address it directly, and `description`/`why`/`doc`/`severity`/`crossingRemedy`/`crossingExcuse` ride the contribution. The two `crossing*` fields own the halves of a crossing finding's `fix`: `crossingRemedy` replaces the default "route shared code through …" opener where relocating the dependency isn't the way out (a one-sided isolation edge has no shared folder to route through), and `crossingExcuse` names the excusal lever that actually works for a pack-shipped edge. Write the remedy into one of these, not into `description` — a rendered finding carries `what`/`why`/`fix`/`doc` and never the rule's description. `gateDir` is the one declarative gate: the rule stays inert until that directory exists in the repo under test (how the baseline's consumer-isolation wall stays quiet pre-flip). The runner hands this pack the active-pack list (`contributedRules` on its manifest, the generic core seam), and [contributed.mjs](contributed.mjs) builds the rules — an undeclared pack contributes nothing, exactly as its own rules would not run. A consumer's local pack contributes the same way. A helper a pack needs beside a barrier (path containment, say) lives in the engine lib (`engine/checks/helpers/path-containment.mjs`), never in this pack's modules.

content.content:
=== dd7ab20 (Jul28) Show dont tell section ===
### Show, don't just tell
- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.

### Interaction cadence
Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.

---
=== current (d6c4c44) ===
### Show, don't just tell
- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
  trustworthy.
- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.

content.content:
1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
7	
8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
15	
16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
27	
28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
30	
31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
35	   it** — do not guess.
36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
50	
51	### Show, don't just tell
52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
60	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
61	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
62	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
63	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
64	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
65	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
66	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
67	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
68	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
69	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
70	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
71	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
72	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
73	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
74	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
75	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
76	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
77	  trustworthy.
78	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
79	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
80	
81	### Interaction cadence
82	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
83	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
84	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
85	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
90	
91	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
92	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
93	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
94	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
95	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
96	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
97	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
98	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
99	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
100	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
101	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
102	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
103	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
104	  loudly.
105	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
106	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
107	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
108	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
109	  are requirements, not incidental.
110	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
111	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
112	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
113	  the review overlays.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
118	
119	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
120	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
121	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
122	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
123	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
124	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
125	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
126	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
127	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
128	  in scope.
129	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
130	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
131	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
132	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
137	
138	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
139	if it improves a metric.
140	
141	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
142	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
143	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
144	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
145	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
146	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
147	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
148	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
149	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
150	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
151	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
152	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
153	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
154	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
155	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
156	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
157	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
158	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
159	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
160	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
161	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
162	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
167	
168	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
169	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
170	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
171	
172	An iteration note captures:
173	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
174	  showed it).
175	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
176	  possible).
177	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
178	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
179	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
180	
181	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
182	
183	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
184	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
185	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
186	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
187	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
188	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
189	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
190	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
191	
192	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
193	
194	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
195	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
196	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
197	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
198	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
199	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
200	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
201	
202	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
203	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
204	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
205	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
206	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
207	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
208	and leave it visible as a known gap.
209	
210	### Definition of done for an accepted change
211	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
212	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
213	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
214	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
215	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
216	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
217	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
218	  changed**.
219	
220	---
221	
222	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
223	
224	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
225	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
226	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
227	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
228	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
229	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
230	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
231	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
232	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
233	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
238	
239	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
240	
241	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
242	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its

244	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
245	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
246	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
247	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
248	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
249	  until someone re-opens the source.

251	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
252	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
253	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
254	  a stated gap is part of that.
255	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
256	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the

265	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
266	
267	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
268	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and

276	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
277	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
278

282	
283	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
284	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
285	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
286	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
287	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.

322	first-class experiments:
323

325	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
326	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family

341	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
342	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
343	
344	---
345	
346	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
347	
348	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
349	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
350	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
351	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
352	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
353	substantially change a sub-step.
354	
355	---
356	
357	## 13. Continuity across sessions
358	
359	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
360	**resumable** state.
361	
362	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
363	  clean checkout.
364	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
365	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
366	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
367	  codebase.

369	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline

371	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
